title: Accessibility basics
summary: Repair a page so it works for screen-reader users: language, alt text, labels, heading order and landmarks.

docs.title: MDN: HTML - a good basis for accessibility

quiz.q: What is the purpose of `lang="en"` on the html element?
options: It translates the page into English
It tells browsers and screen readers the language of the text
quiz.explain: `lang` does not translate anything. It declares the language so software can pronounce and process the text correctly.

quiz.q: Which link text is the most accessible?
quiz.explain: Screen-reader users often list all links on a page, so each link must make sense out of context.

quiz.q: Click the line that breaks the heading order.
quiz.explain: The page jumps from `h2` to `h4`. Use `h3` so the outline has no gaps.

quiz.q: Give this decorative divider image an empty description so screen readers skip it.
quiz.explain: An empty `alt` tells assistive technology the image is decorative. Leaving `alt` out is different, because the file name may be read out.

exercise.task:
The page in `index.html` has several accessibility problems. Fix them.

- Add `lang="en"` to the `<html>` element.
- Give the image a meaningful `alt`.
- Add a `<label for="email">` for the email input (`id="email"`).
- Change the `<h4>` to an `<h3>` so the heading order has no gaps.
- Wrap the page content in a `<main>` element.
- Replace the link text `click here` with text that describes the destination.
hints: Read the page from top to bottom and list what a screen reader would say: language, headings, the image, the field, the link.
You need: lang on html, alt on img, a label whose for matches the input id, h3 instead of h4, a main wrapper, and better link text.
